title: Crossing the flood
hookLine: how did you cross? by not halting and not straining (SN 1.1)

lines: A GLOW IN THE JETA GROVE.
HOW DID YOU CROSS THE FLOOD?
cards: Late at night, a glow fills the Jeta Grove near Savatthi. A deva, a radiant being from the heavens, has come down to see the Buddha.
It bows, stands to one side, and asks the question that opens the whole Connected Sayings. How, dear sir, did you cross the flood?
The flood, in these texts, is everything that sweeps a person along: wanting, becoming, views, not knowing. The answer is a handful of words in Pali, and it sounds like a riddle.

teach.b: The Buddha answers: by not halting, friend, and by not straining, I crossed the flood. The deva asks the obvious thing: how? When I stood still, he says, I sank.

teach.h: I PUSHED AND WAS SWEPT AWAY
teach.b: When I pushed hard, I was swept away. So, not halting and not straining, I crossed.

teach.h: A SWIMMER IN A STRONG RIVER
teach.b: Take a swimmer in a strong river. Stop moving and you go under. Thrash and fight the current and you wear yourself out and get carried off anyway.
What gets you across is steady movement, without either. The Buddhist tradition reads this in many ways.

Some commentators say halting means getting stuck in craving and views, and straining means getting carried away by them. Others hear the middle way of the very first sermon, between indulgence and harsh effort.
Some meditation teachers just hear practical advice: don't quit, don't force. The deva is delighted.

teach.h: THE DEVA'S VERSE, AND IT VANISHES
teach.b: It speaks a verse: after a long time, at last, I see a brahmin, a holy one, fully at peace, who without halting, without straining, has crossed over clinging to the world.
Then it bows, circles the Buddha, and vanishes. That's the whole discourse.
Look back at this week: a warning shouted from a riverbank, parents named as first teachers, effort kept alive, word and deed matched, the short books closed, the Connected Sayings opened.
And now the first of them, back at the water again, with a way across.

how: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions describe balanced effort as neither too tight nor too loose, and the first discourse of the Samyutta Nikaya is sometimes cited when they do.

o: a ford, a safe place to cross
the far shore, beyond the river
a flood that sweeps beings along

s: SN 1.1 is the first discourse of the Connected Sayings
the Samyutta Nikaya opens with the deva's question about crossing the flood.
the Buddha says he crossed by trying as hard as he could
he says pushing hard swept him away; he crossed by not halting and not straining.
all Buddhist commentators read halting and straining the same way
some read craving and views, some the middle way, some teachers simply balanced effort.

games.q: you're a swimmer in a strong river, trying to reach the far bank. what gets you across, according to SN 1.1?
o: stop and float until the current slows.
fight the current with everything you've got.
keep moving steadily, neither stopping nor straining.
games.why: the Buddha says: when I stood still, I sank; when I pushed, I was swept away. the way across was neither.

practice: Let the breath be a river: don't stop it, don't push it.

When you notice you've drifted off into thoughts, that's halting, so gently start moving again by feeling the next breath; when you notice you're gripping, trying hard to breathe well, that's straining, so soften the shoulders, the jaw, the belly.
Not stuck, not forcing: just crossing, one breath at a time.

wordCard.voice: Ogha, the flood. The first discourse of the Connected Sayings: the Buddha crossed without halting and without straining, because standing still sinks and pushing gets swept away. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali ogha: a flood, the current that sweeps beings along.

carryVoice: Your line: not halting, not straining. Steady, the way a swimmer crosses a strong river. That's a week, done.
